passage: With a small loan from his uncle and three weeks before the hostel stall opened, Baljeet sat outside the cafe near the highway and copied its board: tea at fifteen, sandwiches at forty, open from seven to ten at night. 'If it works there, it works here,' he told Mohit, a friend in the hostel. He opened with the same prices and hours. On the first night he sold four teas. The hostel block was quiet after nine, and students there had monthly pocket money, not the stream of passers-by the cafe had. By the end of the week he still had half a tray of sandwiches. Mohit said, 'The cafe has a road outside. We have a corridor.'

qa.q: How many teas did Baljeet sell on the first night?
qa.a: Baljeet sold four teas on the first night.

qa.q: What was Baljeet thinking when he said 'If it works there, it works here'?
qa.a: Baljeet believed the two places were alike enough to copy, and felt confident, though the cafe had a busy road and the stall had a quiet corridor.

qa.q: What other approach could Baljeet use to set prices and hours?
qa.a: Baljeet could ask hostel students what they would buy and when, since a stall for a quiet block needs to fit the people who are actually there.

qa.q: How does Mohit see the stall?
qa.a: Mohit sees the key difference between a road with passers-by and a quiet corridor, and points it out.

grounding: Shows a student copying a cafe's pricing and hours for a hostel stall while ignoring that the cafe sits on a busy road and the stall serves a quiet block.

passage:
Hemant had spent two evenings at the busy café near the college's main gate, notebook open. Cold coffee at eighty rupees, sandwiches at a hundred and twenty, open eleven to eleven. Always full.
"Same prices, same hours," he told his friend Preeti. "If it works for them, it works for me."
His stall opened in the courtyard of the girls' and boys' hostel blocks at the far end of campus. At eleven in the morning, nobody came. The hostellers were in class. At night, the few who came out looked at the prices and walked to the mess.
After two weeks, he had thrown away more sandwiches than he had sold.
Preeti sat with him on the empty bench. "The café is on the main road. Half their customers are office people passing by. You've got forty students who already paid for mess food."
Hemant looked at the unsold tray and said nothing.

qa.q: How much did the café charge for sandwiches?
qa.a: Sandwiches at a hundred and twenty.

qa.q: What might Hemant have been feeling as he looked at the unsold tray?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and embarrassed, realising he had copied a plan built for a completely different crowd.

qa.q: What would you change first in Hemant's stall plan?
qa.a: I would ask hostel students when they are hungry and what they would pay, then set hours and prices to fit them, not the main-road café.

qa.q: How might the hostel students see Hemant's stall?
qa.a: They see prices meant for office workers and hours when they are in class, so the stall feels like it wasn't made for them.

grounding: It shows a student copying a busy café's prices and hours for a stall that serves a quiet hostel block, ignoring the key difference.

"Eleven to seven, same as the corner café," Uday said, setting up the folding table near the hostel block. "And same menu, same prices."
Vishal looked around. "The corner café is on the highway, bro. Trucks, office people, bus stop."
"Food is food."
Day one. Four customers. Day five. Two.
"Where is everyone?" Uday asked.
"In class, till four," Vishal said. "Then they eat at the mess at seven-thirty, because it's already paid for. They're hungry at eleven at night, not at eleven in the morning."
"The café sells so much at lunch."
"Because office people eat lunch there. We don't have office people. We have forty hostel students with no money."
Uday stared at the cooler full of unsold juice. "So I copied the wrong thing."
"You copied the right café. For the wrong place."

qa.q: How many customers came on day five?
qa.a: Two customers came on day five.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling while staring at the cooler of unsold juice?
qa.a: Uday felt deflated and embarrassed, realising the copied plan didn't fit the stall's customers.

qa.q: What else could Uday try with the same stall, and why?
qa.a: Uday could open late at night with cheaper snacks, since Vishal says the hostel students are hungry at eleven at night.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Uday's plan?
qa.a: Vishal sees the key difference from the start, that the café serves highway traffic and office people, and tries to show Uday why the copy fails.

grounding: It shows a student copying a highway café's hours and prices for a stall serving a quiet hostel block, missing the key difference.
